overview: A rough day for the broader market pulled the default account's equity down to $99,721.87, a loss of $803.46 for the day. Open positions: AMD (13 shares, -$720.13 unrealized), GOOGL (31 shares, +$426.97), NVDA (52 shares, -$70.08), TSLA (28 shares, -$702.06). Despite the daily loss, the default account is still running +1.62% ahead of the S&P 500 since tracking began on 2026-07-20 (portfolio -0.28% vs SPY -1.90%) -- it's losing less than the benchmark on a down day, not gaining outright. The Sneaky Pivot account is up +0.23% since 2026-07-28, +1.97% ahead of SPY over that same short window, holding one position: 25 shares of MSFT (see Mistakes & Corrected Actions -- this position exists because of a real bug, not an intentional live trade this session). Two real orders filled today, both at 9:45am CT from the same event: MSFT (25 shares @ $394.49, Sneaky Pivot strategy) and NVDA (52 shares @ $191.19, mean-reversion strategy, a normal and expected fill from the daily autonomous cycle). Of 10 signals generated today, only those 2 executed; the other 8 (four SOFI buy attempts, four MSFT exit attempts) were correctly stopped from executing -- see below for why. The trailing-stop system raised protective stops 14 times today (all on GOOGL and NVDA, both in the default account) as those positions moved in the account's favor, and caught two real problems that needed manual intervention -- also detailed below. No errors were logged.
market_movement: A broadly negative day across the watchlist: SPY -1.74%, QQQ -2.17%. The steepest drops were SOFI -9.56%, META -7.47%, NOK -6.83%, AMD -6.59%, INTC -5.08%, NU -4.43%, NVDA -3.83%, and TSLA -3.79%. Only two tickers gained: MSFT +2.51% and NFLX +1.71%.

mistakes_and_corrections.summary: The most significant issue found in this project to date: a Sneaky Pivot signal that was only ever supposed to be evaluated in dry-run mode actually got filled for real. At 9:45am CT, the existing always-on autonomous trading cycle (a separate, pre-approved daily job that trades the mean-reversion strategy) ran its normal routine -- but as part of that routine, it processes every order sitting in the 'ready to trade' queue, not just its own. A Sneaky Pivot test signal for MSFT happened to be sitting in that same queue from 8 minutes earlier, because the dry-run tool left it there rather than marking it finished. The result: 25 shares of MSFT were bought for real (paper money, but for real), alongside the NVDA trade that was actually supposed to happen that way.
mistakes_and_corrections.corrected_action: First, safety: both the new MSFT position and a same-event NVDA position had protective stop-loss orders that would have silently expired at market close due to a separate, previously-known technical limitation -- both were manually re-secured with stops that don't expire. Then, the root cause: the dry-run tool was changed so that any signal it merely evaluates (without the user explicitly saying 'go live' in that turn) is immediately marked as finished/inactive the moment it's evaluated, so it can never again be picked up and traded for real by anything else. This was verified working for the rest of the day -- four more SOFI buy attempts and four MSFT sell attempts all evaluated correctly in dry-run and were safely marked inactive, none of them executed. The MSFT position bought by mistake is still open as of this report; the strategy has been signaling it should be sold (price has reached its target), but that exit has correctly stayed dry-run-only pending an explicit decision, exactly as intended now.

mistakes_and_corrections.summary: Separately, the trailing-stop protection tool failed to convert two new stop orders (on NVDA and MSFT) from a same-day-only setting to a never-expires setting, hitting a new error message from the broker it hadn't seen before ('cannot be changed for advanced orders') -- both positions were still protected by their original stops the whole time, just not by the intended stronger setting.
mistakes_and_corrections.corrected_action: Cancelled both original stop orders and replaced them with a different, standalone type of stop order that isn't subject to the same limitation, confirming both were live and set to never expire. The trailing-stop tool successfully raised both of these replacement stops multiple times later in the day, confirming the fix held.

mistakes_and_corrections.summary: The trailing-stop check failed outright twice in a row around 4:25-4:28pm CT with a network timeout.
mistakes_and_corrections.corrected_action: Confirmed via a direct connectivity test that this was a general internet outage on the machine running these tools (a request to google.com also failed the same way), not a problem with the broker or this project's code. No position was left unprotected by this -- stop orders already placed with the broker stay active on the broker's side regardless of whether this machine can currently reach the internet. Connectivity returned on its own within about 15 minutes and later cycles ran normally.
